g9-geography-ug1-t1.overview: This lesson introduces geography as a field of study, tracing the word back to its Greek origin and gathering the definitions scholars have proposed. It then examines the very wide scope of geography and its two main branches, physical geography and human geography, together with their specialized sub-fields.
objectives: Define geography using its Greek origin and the definitions given by Eratosthenes and later scholars
Explain what the scope of a discipline means and why the scope of geography is wide
Identify the earth's spheres that geography studies, including the hydrosphere, atmosphere, lithosphere, biosphere and anthroposphere
Distinguish between physical geography and human geography as the two main branches
Classify specialized fields such as geomorphology, climatology and economic geography under the correct branch
g9-geography-ug1-t1.simple: Geography comes from two Greek words: Geo, meaning earth, and Graphos, meaning writing. So at first it simply meant the description of the earth, a definition given by Eratosthenes around 2300 years ago. Today geography has grown far beyond place names. It is the scientific study of the Earth that describes and analyses how physical, biological and human phenomena vary from place to place and over time, and how they interact. Its scope covers the hydrosphere, atmosphere, lithosphere, biosphere and anthroposphere, and it uses modern tools such as GPS and GIS. Geography has two main branches: physical geography, which studies natural features like climate, landforms, soil and vegetation, and human geography, which studies cultures, population, economic activities and political systems.
g9-geography-ug1-t1.detailed:
The meaning of geography. The term first appeared when Greek civilization reached its peak, formed by combining two Greek words: Geo, meaning earth, and Graphos, meaning writing. Eratosthenes, a famous Greek philosopher who lived from 276 to 194 BC, coined the term and defined geography as the field of study that deals with the description of the earth. That definition now looks very general compared with the scope of modern geography.

Later definitions. Many scholars of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries proposed their own definitions. Alexander Von Humboldt (1769-1859) saw geography as a synthesizing discipline that connects the general with the particular through measurement, mapping and a regional emphasis. The Concise Oxford Dictionary of 1964 called it the science of the earth's surfaces. Hartshorne described it as providing an accurate, orderly and rational description of distributions on the earth's surface, while Yeates (1968) saw it as a science that develops and tests theories explaining and predicting the spatial distribution and locations of things and phenomena. What all definitions share is the idea that geography studies the earth, especially its surface.

A widely accepted definition. Because the discipline is dynamic and its scope and methods keep changing, no single definition satisfies all geographers at all times. A widely accepted one states that geography is the scientific study of the Earth that describes and analyses spatial and temporal variations of physical, biological and human phenomena, and their interrelationships and dynamism over the surface of the Earth.

The scope of geography. Scope means how broad or narrow the content of a field of study is. The scope of geography is very wide, though not limitless, and it changes as new discoveries and ideas enter the field. Geography examines features of the hydrosphere (oceans, rivers and lakes), the atmosphere (the air surrounding our planet), the lithosphere (the solid layer of rocks covering the earth's surface), the biosphere (all living organisms in and on the earth's surface) and the anthroposphere (the part of the environment made or modified by humans). It also tackles everyday economic, social, political and ecological problems, and uses modern technology such as computers, GPS and GIS to analyse information and draw accurate conclusions.

Major areas of focus. Among its concerns are the earth, its position in the universe and its movements; the physical features of the earth's surface, the forces that cause them and their variation from place to place; the two-way relationships and interdependence between human beings and their natural environment; weather and climatic conditions of the lower atmosphere and their spatial distribution; the materials that make up the earth and its diverse landforms; and major human economic activities and their environmental impacts. Geography is therefore a holistic discipline of knowledge and research.

Branches of geography. Geography has two main branches. Physical geography studies the distribution of natural features such as climate, landforms, soil, vegetation, surface drainage systems, water resources and animals, along with their causes, effects and interactions. Its specialized sub-fields include climatology, geomorphology, oceanography, biogeography, soil geography, phytogeography and zoogeography. Human geography studies the distribution and influence of human aspects of the world, including cultures, population settlement, economic activities and political systems. Its specialized fields include cultural geography, population geography, economic geography, political geography, urban geography and historical geography.

workedExamples.problem: Using the textbook definition, decide whether checking how rainfall changes from Degahabour to Gambella and from January to July is a task for geography.
workedExamples.given: Geography studies spatial and temporal variations of physical, biological and human phenomena over the earth's surface.
workedExamples.formula: Spatial variation means differences from place to place; temporal variation means differences over time.
workedExamples.substitution: Rainfall differences between two towns are spatial; differences between January and July are temporal.
workedExamples.calculation: Both kinds of variation appear in one question, and rainfall is a physical phenomenon, so the task fits geography's definition.
workedExamples.answer: Yes, it is a geographic task because it examines spatial and temporal variation of a physical phenomenon.

workedExamples.problem: A researcher maps where coffee is grown in Ethiopia and explains why production is concentrated in the southwest. Under which branch and sub-field of geography does this fall?
workedExamples.given: The study deals with an economic activity of humans and its distribution.
workedExamples.formula: Human geography studies human aspects such as economic activities; its sub-field is economic geography.
workedExamples.substitution: Coffee farming is an economic activity, and mapping its location is studying its spatial distribution.
workedExamples.calculation: Since the subject is a human economic activity rather than a natural feature, it belongs to a human sub-branch.

workedExamples.problem: Classify these sub-fields under the correct branch: climatology, urban geography, geomorphology, political geography.
workedExamples.given: Physical geography has sub-fields like climatology and geomorphology; human geography has sub-fields like urban and political geography.
workedExamples.formula: Sub-fields studying natural features belong to physical geography; those studying human aspects belong to human geography.
workedExamples.substitution: Climate and landforms are natural features; cities and political systems are human aspects.
workedExamples.calculation: Climatology and geomorphology examine nature, so they are physical; urban and political geography examine human organization, so they are human.
workedExamples.answer: Physical: climatology, geomorphology. Human: urban geography, political geography.

workedExamples.problem: Why does no single definition of geography satisfy all geographers at all times?
workedExamples.given: Definitions range from Eratosthenes' description of the earth to Yeates' science of spatial distribution theories.
workedExamples.formula: The nature of a definition depends on the dynamic nature of the discipline and changes in its scope and methods.
workedExamples.substitution: Geography's scope and methods of study keep changing as new ideas enter the field.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the discipline itself changes over time and place, definitions also change with it.
workedExamples.answer: Because geography is dynamic: its scope and methods change, so each era proposes definitions matching its own interests.

commonMistakes: Believing geography is only about memorizing place names and capitals.
Thinking the scope of geography is limitless, when the textbook shows it has clear focus areas.
Climatology or soil geography under human geography instead of physical geography.
Economic geography under physical geography instead of human geography.
Writing that geography studies only the whole earth, when most definitions specify the earth's surface.
Saying Eratosthenes was a modern nineteenth or twentieth century scholar.
Confusing GIS with the biosphere, since the words begin with similar letters.
applications: Using GIS to map flood-prone kebeles along the Awash River before the rainy season.
Planning a school vegetable garden by asking how soil and slope differ from place to place on the compound.
Understanding Ethiopia's position in the Nile Basin through geography's focus on human-environment relationships.
Explaining why coffee grows in Jimma but not in the Ogaden lowlands using cause-effect reasoning.
Following weather forecasts with an awareness that geography studies the lower atmosphere and its variation.
Recognising that GPS locator work used by surveyors and taxi drivers comes from geographic techniques.
g9-geography-ug1-t1.summary: Geography comes from the Greek words Geo (earth) and Graphos (writing) and was first defined by Eratosthenes as the description of the earth. Today it is the scientific study of the Earth that describes and analyses spatial and temporal variations of physical, biological and human phenomena and their interrelationships. Its wide but not limitless scope spans the five spheres of the environment, and it divides into two main branches, physical geography and human geography, each with specialized sub-fields.

g9-geography-ug1-t2.overview: This lesson describes Ethiopia's location in two ways, relative and absolute, and presents the country's areal size compared with its neighbors. It then explains Ethiopia's compact shape, the three theoretical indicators of compactness, and the advantages and disadvantages that size and shape bring to the country.
objectives: Express the relative location of Ethiopia through its vicinal location and strategic location
State the absolute location of Ethiopia using latitudes and longitudes and identify its extreme points
Describe the size of Ethiopia and compare it with the sizes of its neighbors
Explain the three theoretical indicators of compactness and interpret Ethiopia's index of compactness
Analyse the effects of Ethiopia's size and compact shape on its sociocultural, political and economic conditions
g9-geography-ug1-t2.simple: Location can be expressed in two ways. Relative location describes a place in relation to other features: vicinal location shows Ethiopia in relation to its six neighbors, while strategic location describes its position near water bodies and landmasses. Absolute location uses latitude and longitude: Ethiopia lies between 3N and 15N and between 33E and 48E. Ethiopia is the tenth largest country in Africa with 1,106,000 square kilometers, about 0.7 percent of the world's land and 3.6 percent of Africa's landmass. Its shape is more or less compact, or nearly circular, because its north-south and east-west spans are similar. A compact shape gives military and economic advantages, but the large size also brings costly administration, defence needs and infrastructure demands.
g9-geography-ug1-t2.detailed:
Relative location. Relative location refers to the position of a place in relation to the location of other geographic features. It is expressed in two ways. Vicinal location shows the location of a country in relation to its neighboring countries, while strategic location, also called natural or global location, describes a country's position in reference to water bodies and landmasses.

Ethiopia's neighbors. Ethiopia is a landlocked country surrounded by six neighbors and shares a total boundary line of 5,260 km. The lengths are: Eritrea 840 km (Ethiopia lies south of Eritrea), Somalia 1,600 km (west and northwest of Somalia), Kenya 760 km (north of Kenya), Djibouti 310 km (west of Djibouti), Sudan 744 km (east and southeast of Sudan) and South Sudan 1,006 km (northeast of South Sudan). The longest boundary is with Somalia and the shortest is with Djibouti.

Strategic and absolute location. Strategically, Ethiopia is found in northeastern (Horn) Africa, southwest of the Asian continent, in the Nile Basin, south of Europe, northwest of the Indian Ocean, southwest of the Red Sea and south of the Mediterranean Sea. Absolute or astronomical location is expressed as a geographical extent in latitudes and longitudes: Ethiopia lies between 3N and 15N latitudes and 33E and 48E longitudes. Its extreme points are the northern tip of Tigray in the north, Moyalle in the south (Borena), Akobo in the west (Gambella) and the tip of Ogaden in the east.

Size. Ethiopia is the tenth largest country in Africa with a total area of 1,106,000 square kilometers, about 0.7 percent of the world's land area and 3.6 percent of Africa's landmass. Sudan is about 1.01 times bigger (1,849,233 sq km), while Somalia is 1.73 times, South Sudan 1.75 times, Kenya 1.91 times, Eritrea 9.42 times and Djibouti almost 50 times smaller than Ethiopia. Being the largest country in the Horn, combined with a large population, confers many advantages to Ethiopia in the Horn area.

Shape. Countries vary in shape: some are nearly circular or compact, others elongated or linear, others truncated. Ethiopia has a more or less compact shape because its extreme north-south and east-west spans cover comparable distances. The three theoretical indicators of compactness are the boundary-circumference ratio (B/C), the area-boundary ratio (A/B) and the actual-area-to-inscribing-circle ratio (A/A'). Values near 1, or between 0.5 and 1.5, indicate approximate compactness; values approaching 0 indicate elongation or truncation. The larger the areal size per unit of boundary length in the A/B ratio, the more compact the country.

Measuring Ethiopia's compactness. Using the B/C ratio: the boundary is 5,260 km, and the circumference of a circle with an area equal to Ethiopia's (1,106,000 sq km) is computed from A = pi x r squared, giving r = 593.5 km, so C = 2 x 3.14 x 593.5 = 3727.18 km. The ratio is 5260 / 3727.18 = 1.411, meaning Ethiopia's shape deviates about 41 percent from a perfect circle. Because 1.411 lies within the 0.5 to 1.5 band, the shape is considered approximately compact.

Advantages and disadvantages. The large size gives Ethiopia diverse agro-ecological zones with a wide variety of fauna and flora, a large amount of arable land, a great variety of mineral resources and a home for diverse ethnic groups. The compact shape has a military advantage: in the A/B ratio, each 1 km of border safeguarded by the national army protects about 210 sq km of hinterland from enemy assault. However, the large size forces Ethiopia to spend heavily on administration, maintain a large army to protect its sovereignty, find great financial power for infrastructure, and struggle with effective administration and socio-economic integration.

keyTerms.def: The position of a place in relation to the location of other geographic features, expressed as vicinal or strategic location.
The astronomical position of a place expressed as a geographical extent in latitudes and longitudes.
The location of a country in relation to its neighboring countries.
Also called natural or global location; a country's position in reference to water bodies and landmasses.
A nearly circular shape in which the north-south and east-west spans cover comparable distances.
A linear shape in which one dimension of a country greatly exceeds the other, diverging from compactness.
A ratio such as boundary over circumference (B/C), area over boundary (A/B) or area over inscribing-circle area (A/A') used to measure how compact a country's shape is.
Imaginary lines used to express absolute location; for Ethiopia 3N-15N and 33E-48E.

workedExamples.problem: Using Table 1.1, describe the vicinal location of Ethiopia in relation to South Sudan and identify the neighbor with the shortest boundary.
workedExamples.given: Boundary lengths: Somalia 1,600 km; South Sudan 1,006 km; Eritrea 840 km; Kenya 760 km; Sudan 744 km; Djibouti 310 km.
workedExamples.formula: Vicinal location expresses a country's position relative to each neighboring country.
workedExamples.substitution: Ethiopia lies northeast of South Sudan, and Djibouti has only 310 km of shared boundary.
workedExamples.calculation: Comparing all six lengths, 1,600 is the largest and 310 the smallest.
workedExamples.answer: Ethiopia is northeast of South Sudan, and Djibouti shares the shortest boundary line with it.

workedExamples.problem: Compute the boundary-circumference ratio of Ethiopia and state what it implies about the country's shape.
workedExamples.given: Total boundary length = 5,260 km; area of Ethiopia = 1,106,000 sq km; pi = 3.14.
workedExamples.formula: B/C ratio, where C is the circumference of a circle with an area equal to Ethiopia's (C = 2 x pi x r, and r comes from A = pi x r squared).
workedExamples.substitution: pi x r squared = 1,106,000, so r squared = 352,229.3 and r = 593.5 km.
workedExamples.answer: The ratio is 1.411, so Ethiopia's shape deviates about 41 percent from a perfect circle but still lies in the 0.5 - 1.5 band, making it approximately compact.

workedExamples.problem: How many times smaller than Ethiopia is Eritrea, and which neighbor is almost 50 times smaller?
workedExamples.given: Ethiopia's area is 1,106,000 sq km; Eritrea is 118,000 sq km; Djibouti is 23,200 sq km (CSA, 2012).
workedExamples.formula: Size comparison: divide Ethiopia's area by the neighbor's area.
workedExamples.calculation: Eritrea's figure matches the textbook's 9.42 times smaller, and Djibouti's rounds to about 50 times smaller.
workedExamples.answer: Eritrea is 9.42 times smaller than Ethiopia, and Djibouti is almost 50 times smaller.

commonMistakes: Mixing up vicinal and strategic location: vicinal concerns neighboring countries, strategic concerns water bodies and landmasses.
Writing that Ethiopia borders the Red Sea, when it is landlocked and only lies southwest of the Red Sea.
Stating that Sudan shares the longest boundary with Ethiopia, when the longest is with Somalia (1,600 km).
Confusing the extreme points, for example placing Moyalle in the west instead of the south (Borena).
Interpreting a B/C ratio of 1.411 as meaning the shape is elongated, when it indicates approximate compactness.
Forgetting that absolute location needs both latitude (3N-15N) and longitude (33E-48E).
Claiming a large size brings only advantages, when it also raises administrative, defence and infrastructure costs.
applications: Reading a wall map to locate Ethiopia between 3N-15N and 33E-48E and naming its six neighbors.
Explaining Ethiopia's geopolitical influence in the Horn of Africa using its large size and population.
Understanding why border security matters by applying the idea that each 1 km of border protects about 210 sq km of hinterland.
Linking Ethiopia's diverse agro-ecological zones to its farmer diversity, from Borena pastoralists to Gonder teff farmers.
Using strategic location reasoning to see how Ethiopia connects the Red Sea route, the Nile Basin and the Indian Ocean.
Planning road and electricity networks by weighing how a large area raises construction costs.
g9-geography-ug1-t2.summary: Ethiopia's relative location makes it a landlocked country bordered by six neighbors, with its longest boundary (1,600 km) shared with Somalia and its strategic position in northeastern Africa near the Red Sea route. In absolute terms it lies between 3N-15N and 33E-48E, and it is Africa's tenth largest country at 1,106,000 square kilometers. Its compact, nearly circular shape, with a compactness index of 1.411, supports defence and integration but its large size also demands expensive administration and infrastructure.

g9-geography-ug1-t3.overview: This lesson follows Ethiopia's geological history through the four eras of the geological time scale, from the Precambrian to the Cenozoic, and identifies the rocks and structures each era produced. It then uses endogenic and exogenic forces to explain the major landforms of Ethiopia, from Ras Dashen to the Dallol depression and the three physiographic divisions.
objectives: Explain the geological time scale and the four major geological eras in chronological order
Describe the major geological events of the Precambrian, Paleozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic eras in Ethiopia and the Horn
Match the sedimentary rocks Adigrat sandstone, Hintalo limestone and Upper Sandstone to their periods of formation
Distinguish endogenic and exogenic forces as the two opposite forces that created Ethiopia's landforms
Outline the three physiographic divisions of Ethiopia and their principal highland and lowland units
g9-geography-ug1-t3.simple: Geologists measure Earth's history with the geological time scale, which has four eras. The Precambrian, from 4.5 billion to 600 million years ago, is the oldest and longest, producing Ethiopia's old crystalline basement complex rock through intensive volcanic and orogenic activity. In the Paleozoic, denudation and peneplanation dominated, leaving a gap in the rock record. The Mesozoic saw the land sink and rise, forming sedimentary rocks: Adigrat sandstone in the Triassic, Hintalo limestone in the Jurassic and Upper Sandstone in the Cretaceous. In the Cenozoic, uplifting and lava flows built the highlands and the Great East African Rift Valley formed. The landforms of Ethiopia, from the 4,620 m Ras Dashen down to the Dallol depression 116 m below sea level, result from internal endogenic forces and surface exogenic forces.
g9-geography-ug1-t3.detailed:
The geological time scale. To describe the geology and history of life on Earth, scientists developed the geological time scale, which involves four major geological eras. Each era is judged by three characteristics: the relative positions of the continents, the character of the prevailing climate and the predominant lifeform. In chronological order the eras are the Precambrian (4.5 billion to 600 million years ago), the Paleozoic (600 million to 250 million years ago), the Mesozoic (250 million to 70 million years ago) and the Cenozoic (70 million years ago to the recent time).

The Precambrian Era. This is the oldest and longest era, covering about 5/6 of the earth's geological time. Events in the Horn included frequent orogenic movements, intensive volcanic activities, denudation in the later periods and the formation of folded mountains. The first forms of life emerged, such as one-celled amoeba and jellyfish, and the oldest rock, the old crystalline basement complex, formed beneath all other rocks. Due to continuous denudation its outcrops appear in central and northern Tigray, in Metekel, Assossa, Illubabor and the Abbay Gorge, in central Sidama, southern Omo, southern Bale and Borena, and in central, western and northern Eritrea.

The Paleozoic Era. In Ethiopia the major geomorphic process was denudation followed by peneplanation, and no significant structural formation took place, so this is the only era that left a gap in rock formation in Ethiopia. The massive denudation formed inselbergs, residual features, in some parts of the country. Invertebrates dominated life during this era.

The Mesozoic Era. This era was marked by alternate slow sinking and uplifting of the landmass, called epeirogenesis. It was the era of sedimentary rock formation, divided into the Triassic (250-180 million years), Jurassic (180-135 million) and Cretaceous (135-70 million). In the Triassic the land sank and a sea transgressed into today's Somalia and southeastern Ethiopia, forming the Adigrat sandstone, the oldest sedimentary rock. In the Jurassic the transgression continued northwestward, depositing Hintalo limestone. In the Cretaceous the land began to rise and the sea regressed southeast, depositing Upper Sandstone, the youngest sedimentary rock, which overlies the rest. The Mesozoic is known for reptiles such as dinosaurs, but at its end the dinosaurs disappeared and mammals, birds and flowering plants emerged. The Mesozoic sediments were later buried by Cenozoic igneous rocks but are exposed today in the southeastern lowlands, central Tigray and the Abbay and Wabishebelle gorges.

The Cenozoic Era. In the Tertiary Period (70 million to 2 million years ago), the uplifting begun in the Cretaceous reached its maximum, forming a huge dome, and great cracks released extensive basaltic lava, the Trappean lava series, which formed the Northwestern Highlands, the Southeastern Highlands and the Somali plateaus. Continued cracking and faulting formed the Great East African Rift Valley System, of which the Ethiopian Rift Valley is part: it stretches from Palestine-Jordan in the north to Malawi-Mozambique in the south, about 7,200 km in total, of which 5,600 km is in Africa and 1,700 km in Eritrea and Ethiopia. In the Quaternary Period (2 million years ago to recent), volcanism produced the Afar Horst extending into Djibouti, the active volcano of Ertalle in Afar, the dormant volcano Fentalle in Eastern Oromia, the lava fields of Metahara, and thermal springs and fumaroles of the rift valley, along with pluvial rainfall and deposition in the lowlands. Modern humans evolved during the Quaternary.

Landforms of Ethiopia. Landform means an individual earth surface feature, and Ethiopia's are largely the result of Cenozoic tectonic and volcanic activity. They reflect two opposite forces: the endogenic force from inside the earth, such as volcanic and tectonic activity, and the exogenic force at the surface, such as denudation and peneplanation. Altitude varies from about 116 meters below sea level at the Dallol depression (Kobar Sink) to 4,620 m above sea level at Ras Dashen in the Semein mountain system. With 1,000 m as the dividing contour, 56 percent of the land is highland, earning Ethiopia the name 'Roof of Eastern Africa'. The relief divides into three physiographic divisions: the Western Highlands and Associated Lowlands (44 percent of the area, drained by the Abbay, Baro and Tekezze, with sub-divisions of the Plateau of Tigray, the North Central Massif, the Plateau of Shewa and the Southwestern Highlands), the Southeastern Highlands and Associated Lowlands (the Hararghe plateaus, Arsi plateau, Bale Massif and Sidama highlands, sources of the Wabe Shebelle and Genale rivers), and the Rift Valley, which runs diagonally from the Afar Triangle in the north, through the Main Ethiopian Rift or Lakes' Region, to the Chew-Bahir Rift in the south.

keyTerms.def: A scale developed by scientists to describe the geology and history of life on Earth, involving four major geological eras divided into periods, epochs and years.
A major division of geological time; the four eras are Precambrian, Paleozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic.
The force originating from inside the earth, such as volcanic activity and tectonic forces, that builds landforms.
The force originating at the earth's surface, such as denudation and peneplanation, that wears landforms down.
The spread of a sea over the land, as in the Triassic and Jurassic marine invasions of southeastern Ethiopia.
The retreat of a sea from the land, as when the sea pulled back southeast in the Cretaceous.
Alternate slow sinking and uplifting of the landmass, the process that marked the Mesozoic Era.
Mountain building by folding and volcanic eruption, frequent during the Precambrian Era.
The physical shape of the land surface; the relief of Ethiopia is divided into three physiographic divisions.

workedExamples.problem: Match each sedimentary rock to the correct period: Adigrat sandstone, Hintalo limestone, Upper Sandstone.
workedExamples.given: Adigrat sandstone formed when the sea first transgressed in the Triassic; Hintalo limestone formed during continued transgression in the Jurassic; Upper Sandstone formed during sea regression in the Cretaceous.
workedExamples.formula: Rock type corresponds to period: Triassic 250-180 million years, Jurassic 180-135 million, Cretaceous 135-70 million.
workedExamples.substitution: Transgression in the Triassic gives Adigrat sandstone; Jurassic transgression gives Hintalo limestone; Cretaceous regression gives Upper Sandstone.
workedExamples.calculation: Arranging the rocks in order of formation from oldest to youngest confirms the sequence.
workedExamples.answer: Adigrat sandstone - Triassic; Hintalo limestone - Jurassic; Upper Sandstone - Cretaceous.

workedExamples.problem: Why are sandstones and limestones seen as surface outcrops in the Plateau of Tigray?
workedExamples.given: The Plateau of Tigray is composed largely of sandstones and limestones from the Mesozoic Era.
workedExamples.formula: Exogenic forces wear down the surface; the overlying basalt of the Tertiary lava has been eroded away.
workedExamples.substitution: Where overlying basalt covers the sediments they are hidden; where denudation removes the basalt, the older rocks are exposed.
workedExamples.calculation: Continuous denudation in Tigray stripped the cap, so the older sedimentary rocks appear on the surface.
workedExamples.answer: Because the overlying basaltic rock has been eroded by exogenic denudation, exposing the older sandstones and limestones.

workedExamples.problem: Which era is most significant for the formation of the present landforms of Ethiopia, and why?
workedExamples.given: The Trappean lava built the Northwestern and Southeastern Highlands and the Somali plateaus; faulting then formed the Ethiopian Rift Valley; Quaternary volcanoes appeared in Afar.
workedExamples.formula: The era whose tectonic and volcanic activities produced today's relief is the most significant.
workedExamples.substitution: All these events happened in the Cenozoic Era, in its Tertiary and Quaternary periods.
workedExamples.calculation: Since the highlands, the Rift Valley and recent volcanoes all date from Cenozoic events, that era dominates the present landscape.
workedExamples.answer: The Cenozoic Era: Tertiary uplifting and lava flows built the highlands, and faulting formed the rift system, with Quaternary volcanism adding recent features.

workedExamples.problem: The textbook says the Hintalo limestone in the northwest is younger while it is older in the southeast. Explain this using the direction of transgression.
workedExamples.given: During the Jurassic, the sea transgressed from the southeast into the mainland in the northwest direction.
workedExamples.formula: Rock age follows the direction of marine transgression: areas flooded first hold the oldest sediments.
workedExamples.substitution: The southeast was submerged first, so its Jurassic deposit is older; the northwest was reached later, so its limestone is younger.
workedExamples.calculation: Following the northwestward spread of the sea, the sediments become progressively younger towards the northwest.
workedExamples.answer: Because the sea advanced northwestward, deposition in the southeast preceded deposition in the northwest, making the northwest limestone younger.

commonMistakes: Placing the formation of the Rift Valley in the Mesozoic Era, when it formed during the Tertiary Period of the Cenozoic.
Saying sedimentary rock formation occurred in the Precambrian, when the Mesozoic was the era of sedimentary rock formation.
Thinking the Paleozoic left major structures in Ethiopia, when it was the only era that left a gap in rock formation.
Reversing the rock ages: Adigrat sandstone is the oldest sedimentary rock and Upper Sandstone the youngest.
Mixing transgression with regression: transgression is the sea spreading over the land, regression is its retreat.
Writing that Ras Dashen is 4,620 m below sea level or that Dallol is above sea level, when Ras Dashen is the highest point and the Dallol depression (Kobar Sink) lies 116 m below sea level.
Attributing landforms only to endogenic forces, when exogenic forces such as denudation also shaped them.
applications: Reading a geological map of Ethiopia to find Precambrian outcrops in central and northern Tigray.
Explaining why salt plains and Lake Assale in the Afar Triangle exist in a former volcanic rift zone.
Using the Semein mountains and Ras Dashen for tourism planning as part of geography's study of landforms.
Connecting the volcanic soils of the western and southeastern highlands to Ethiopia's productive agriculture.
Understanding why the Afar Triangle's fossil-rich sediments reveal ancient ancestors of primates and hominids.
Avoiding settlements near active volcanic features such as Ertalle when planning development in Afar.
g9-geography-ug1-t3.summary: Ethiopia's geology spans four eras: the Precambrian formed the old crystalline basement complex rock, the Paleozoic was a time of denudation with a gap in the rock record, the Mesozoic produced transgressed sedimentary rocks from Adigrat sandstone to Upper Sandstone, and the Cenozoic built the highlands and carved the Great East African Rift Valley. The present landforms, from Ras Dashen at 4,620 m to the Kobar Sink at 116 m below sea level, are the combined work of endogenic and exogenic forces, organized into three physiographic divisions: the Western Highlands and lowlands, the Southeastern Highlands and lowlands, and the Rift Valley.

events.label: Precambrian
events.detail: 4.5 billion - 600 million years ago: folded mountains, basement complex rock

events.label: Paleozoic
events.detail: 600 - 250 million years ago: denudation and peneplanation, gap in rock record

events.label: Mesozoic
events.detail: 250 - 70 million years ago: Adigrat sandstone, Hintalo limestone, Upper Sandstone

events.label: Cenozoic
events.detail: 70 million years ago - recent: highlands from Trappean lava, East African Rift Valley, Quaternary volcanoes

questions.q: Which era is the oldest and longest, covering about 5/6 of the earth's geological time?
questions.explanation: The Precambrian Era extends from 4.5 billion to 600 million years ago and is the oldest and longest.

questions.q: The oldest sedimentary rock formed in Ethiopia during the Mesozoic Era is:
questions.explanation: Adigrat sandstone formed in the Triassic Period and is the oldest sedimentary rock.

questions.q: The Great East African Rift Valley extends about 7,200 km from Palestine-Jordan to Malawi-Mozambique.
questions.explanation: The rift system stretches from Palestine-Jordan in the north to Malawi-Mozambique in the south, about 7,200 km, of which 1,700 km is in Eritrea and Ethiopia.

questions.q: Which era is known for the predominance of invertebrates in Ethiopia and the Horn?
questions.explanation: During the Paleozoic Era the major process was denudation and invertebrates dominated.

questions.q: Explain the difference between endogenic and exogenic forces and give one example of each.
questions.answer: endogenic: inside the earth, volcanic or tectonic|exogenic: surface, denudation or peneplanation
questions.explanation: Endogenic forces originate inside the earth, for example volcanic and tectonic activity; exogenic forces originate at the surface, for example denudation and peneplanation.

questions.q: The Afar Horst and the active volcano of Ertalle were formed during the:
questions.explanation: The Quaternary Period of the Cenozoic produced the Afar Horst, the Ertalle volcano, Fentalle and the Metahara lava fields.

questions.q: During the Triassic Period, the landmass sank and the sea transgressed into today's Somalia and southeastern Ethiopia.
questions.explanation: In the Triassic, sinking of the land was followed by the transgression of a nearby sea into Somalia and southeastern Ethiopia.

questions.q: Name the highest mountain peak of Ethiopia and its approximate elevation.
questions.explanation: Ras Dashen in the Semein mountain system rises to 4,620 m above mean sea level.

questions.q: Why do geologists say the Paleozoic Era left a gap in the rock formation of Ethiopia?
questions.answer: denudation and peneplanation|no structural formation or sedimentation
questions.explanation: In the Paleozoic, denudation followed by peneplanation dominated and no significant structural formation took place, so no rock record was laid down.

questions.q: Arrange the geological eras from oldest to youngest.
questions.explanation: The order is Precambrian, Paleozoic, Mesozoic, Cenozoic.

questions.q: Describe the two main geological events of the Tertiary Period in Ethiopia.
questions.answer: uplifting and Trappean lava built the highlands|rifting formed the Great East African Rift Valley
questions.explanation: Tertiary uplifting reached its maximum and cracks released Trappean basaltic lava forming the Northwestern and Southeastern Highlands and Somali plateaus; continued faulting formed the Great East African Rift Valley System.
